title: 20 Years of Readiness: How Target Supports Team Members and Communities Before, During and After Disasters
summary: Learn how Target is strengthening our local communities across the country before, during and after disasters strike and how our Corporate Command Center empowers us to take action instantly.
body_text: As hurricane season begins, Target is doing what it has done for nearly two decades: preparing early, staying ready and showing up when it matters most. Disaster readiness is just one of the ways Target brings our enterprise strategy to life — strengthening teams and communities by showing up for guests, team members and neighbors in moments that matter. Supporting our team is the foundation of everything we do. We believe that when team members are prepared in advance of severe weather and other disasters, they are better equipped to support our guests and communities and recover more quickly. That’s why Target provides preparedness tips to help team members and their families stay safe, conducts drills throughout the year and offers care sites and crisis support when disasters strike. And when team members are directly impacted, the Team Member Giving Fund can provide financial assistance to help them take care of basic needs and recover. Preparing and supporting our team members is also a critical part of ensuring Target is ready to serve guests and communities before severe weather arrives. Through ongoing investments, strong partnerships and a nationwide network of stores and supply chain facilities, Target helps ensure communities have what they need ahead of severe weather. Essentials like water, batteries, food and flashlights are proactively positioned closer to where they’re needed, helping stores stay stocked and ready to serve. Teams also pre-position mobile charging stations and generators — resources that can provide both critical support and a sense of normalcy during uncertain times. At the heart of this effort is Target’s Corporate Command Center, or C3. Founded in 2006, C3 has monitored global events 24/7 for 20 years, tracking severe weather and other incidents that could affect guests, team members and communities. By keeping teams informed and connected, C3 helps Target prepare ahead, respond quickly and adapt as conditions change. When a disaster hits, the work shifts quickly from preparation to response and recovery. Target teams leverage our vast network across stores, our supply chain and partners to move the pre-positioned pallets of supplies at facilities located near the markets where they’re needed most. But just as important is what happens next. Long after headlines fade, Target continues supporting recovery efforts — whether that’s through volunteerism, providing much-needed supplies or helping communities rebuild. That care continues to show up in meaningful ways. After Hurricane Helene, for example, team members stepped in to provide hot meals and distribute fuel to fellow team members in need, demonstrating how Team Target comes together to make a difference for one another. Target also invests $2.5 million annually in disaster relief efforts, supporting organizations like the American Red Cross and Strongward (formally known as SBP) to help communities access food, financial assistance, medicine and other essentials. Since 2024, we have provided more than $5.7 million in one-time donations to support long-term recovery efforts for communities impacted by natural disasters. We donated $250,000 to Appalachia Service Project to rebuild damaged homes as part of our $3 million Hurricane Helene commitment . And in 2025, Target’s volunteer teams were on the ground with Convoy of Hope in Kerrville, Texas, to assist families who were still impacted after the severe floods there and partnered in California with Brotherhood Crusade after the devastating Pasadena wildfires. As this year’s hurricane season gets underway, Target continues to invest in the partnerships, preparedness and capabilities that make this work possible. Because when communities are stronger, everyone is stronger — and that’s something worth preparing for every day.

title: How to build a customer profile for better targeting
summary: Build a customer profile your team will actually use. A 5-step framework with examples, common mistakes, and tools to keep profiles current as buyers shift.
body_text: Your customer profile is probably wrong, and that's fine—as long as you know it. Most B2B teams build a profile during a kickoff workshop, plug it into a slide deck, and treat it like a fossil for the next two years while their actual customers change jobs, switch budgets, and stop caring about the things the profile says they care about. The teams that win treat customer profiles as living documents—reviewed quarterly, updated with real CRM data, and tied to the workflows that depend on them. In this guide, I'll walk you through what a customer profile is, how to build one from scratch, and the tools that keep profiles in sync with reality. Table of contents: What is a customer profile? How to build a customer profile Types of customer profile tools to help you stop guessing Common customer profile mistakes Give your customer profiles new life with Zapier What is a customer profile? A customer profile is a data-backed description of a customer or customer segment most likely to buy from your business. It brings together shared traits like needs, behaviors, goals, and buying habits so you can create more relevant marketing, better products, and a smoother customer experience . Customer profiling helps teams understand buyer needs and target their best-fit audience more effectively. Notice I said "best-fit," not "fantasy buyer you made up in your head who has unlimited budget and no questions and definitely won't churn after three months." Customer profiles are a map, not a vision board. And without one, you're spending your marketing budget like a drunk person at Target—everything looks good, nothing fits, and you're crying in the parking lot. A customer profile typically leans on three pillars: Demographics (or firmographics for B2B) are quantifiable characteristics that tell you who your target audience is, such as job titles, industry, company size, and region. Buying motivations explain why that segment buys—the shared priorities, pressures, and trigger events that move a best-fit account from "we're fine" to "we need this now." Behavioral data describes how they engage with your brand—purchase history, channel preferences, login frequency, features touched, support tickets opened, and loyalty. Customer profile vs. buyer persona These get used interchangeably, but they serve different purposes. Confusing them is a bit like confusing a weather forecast with a specific person who owns an umbrella. Related, but not interchangeable. A customer profile (sometimes called an ideal customer profile, or ICP) is a representation of an optimal buying segment or account . It's built on quantitative parameters, firmographics, or demographics, such as headcount, industry vertical, revenue bands, location, and purchase frequency. The customer profile typically lives inside your CDP (customer data platform) or CRM as a single source of truth. It identifies precisely where your team should focus its efforts. In contrast, a buyer persona shifts the focus to the individual stakeholders within the customer profile. These semi-fictional archetypes map out the psychographics, motivations, and pain points of specific people—like the end user or the executive signer—you need to convince once you have your foot in the door. Because B2B buying committees can easily reach 10+ stakeholders, a single customer profile will require several distinct buyer personas to help growth and content teams design tailored messaging. A buyer persona tells you how to communicate once you're in the door. How to build a customer profile Most templates only capture surface-level details, which is how you end up with a profile that could describe half your industry. A profile worth using is built on real data, real behavior, and real buying signals. Here's a simple five-step framework. 1. Identify your "Goldilocks" customers Demographics alone are basically astrology for marketers. "She's a weekend hiker with a penchant for morning journaling" tells you as much about your customer's buying behavior as knowing her favorite "Real Housewives" franchise. (It's Atlanta, obviously, because she has taste.) Instead, look for customers who sit at the intersection of high lifetime value (LTV) and high Net Promoter Score (NPS) . These are the ones who pay more, stay longer, and use the product naturally in their daily workflow with little support. Pull the top 10 to 15 customers based on LTV and NPS, then look for patterns, like industry, team size at the time of purchase, how they found you, and what they did in the first 30 days. The point is to pattern-match on customers who already see your product as essential—not chase leads that look big on paper and churn six months in. 2. Talk to real customers to understand why they buy Spreadsheets can tell you what's happening, but they're absolutely useless at telling you why it's happening. And industry reports tell you what everyone is doing on average, which is the least useful possible frame for your specific buyer in your specific segment with your specific problem. Get on calls with a handful of the Goldilocks customers from step 1 and dig into the triggers that pushed them to buy. Twenty minutes with a real customer beats months of staring at the dashboard. Avoid generic questions. Instead, ask questions like: What was the specific moment you realized you needed a solution like ours? What was the biggest hurdle you faced during implementation? If you had to cancel tomorrow, which feature would you miss most? Who else in your organization had to sign off, and what were their concerns? The first question alone usually surfaces a trigger event you can't get any other way, and trigger events are the single most useful thing in a profile. Just remember that you're pattern-matching across your best-fit accounts, so a recurring trigger is a profile input, and one memorable answer is just an anecdote. 3. Document the buying journey There's the customer journey you imagine and the one that actually happened. They're rarely the same, and your attribution model is usually the last to find out. A buyer might look like an organic search lead in your dashboard when in reality they saw a LinkedIn ad a month ago, mentioned it to a friend who's already a customer, listened to the friend rave about you for 10 unbroken minutes at a happy hour, and then Googled you the day they were ready to buy. The dashboard says "organic." The actual story is "social → word of mouth → branded search." The dashboard is, once again, lying to you. Pair your analytics (GA4 or whatever you're using—I'm not opening that can of worms today) with your CRM history to map the actual touchpoints. Once you do, you can see where customers spent time before buying, what content they engaged with, and how long the path took. That's what tells you where to invest in content, what questions Sales should ask early, and which channels are doing real work versus just taking credit at the end of the quarter. 4. Synthesize the data into a one-page cheat sheet If your customer profile is 10 pages long, no one will read it. Documents that long are often created by people who have mistaken length for usefulness. Your goal should be a one-page cheat sheet that someone can scan in 30 seconds. It should feel like a quick reference, not a full story. Here are a few ideas to include: Segment snapshot: The firmographic traits your best-fit accounts share—industry, company size, tech stack, etc. Core problem: The main issue this segment is trying to solve Trigger event: The specific nightmare that pushes these accounts to start looking for a solution right now Dealbreaker: The one thing that disqualifies a fit, like a missing integration, a price ceiling, or no SSO Anti-fit: Who to skip—the low-budget, high-support, wrong-stack accounts that look great on paper and churn in 180 days Build it that way, and the team will actually use it. Build it any longer, and you've made a decorative artifact for a Notion page nobody will ever scroll to the bottom of. 5. Automate your customer profiling The biggest mistake teams make is treating a customer profile like a static portrait. (Customers have an irritating habit of continuing to exist after you've documented them.) With Zapier , you can enrich profiles automatically. For example, route Typeform survey responses into HubSpot or Salesforce contact records, pull firmographic data into a central database when a new lead lands, or trigger a Slack alert the moment a best-fit prospect submits a demo request. Every behavioral signal flows into the profile pillars without anyone having to touch a spreadsheet. Types of customer profile tools to help you stop guessing Building an accurate customer profile isn't something a single tool can do on its own. It requires data from multiple sources working together. But the right stack makes the process faster, cleaner, and considerably less painful. Here are some common categories of customer profile tools worth modeling: AI orchestration : A tool like Zapier automates every part of the workflow below, syncing form submissions into your CRM, firing enrichment when a lead lands, updating scores when behavior shifts, and pinging the right rep the second a profile crosses a threshold. CRM : The foundation of the whole system. Your CRM is where customer data lives and evolves over time as new interactions, purchases, and activities are recorded. Lead enrichment : These tools add firmographic, demographic, and contact data, turning incomplete records into more useful customer profiles. Sales automation : Sales reps should spend their time talking to prospects, not filling in blanks by hand or Googling prospects between calls. Customer engagement : Post-purchase interactions provide valuable behavioral data that enriches customer profiles long after the initial sale. Lead scoring : This transforms profile data into a prioritization signal, helping sales teams focus on the prospects most likely to convert. Marketing automation : Rather than treating every lead the same, marketing automation makes it possible to act on profile segments at scale with personalized campaigns and messaging. Analytics and business intelligence tools : These tools uncover patterns in customer behavior, helping refine profiles and improve targeting over time. Common customer profile mistakes Once you've audited enough CRM setups you know that even with the best intentions, customer profiles drift. If you aren't careful, your data-driven blueprint can turn into a cluttered junk drawer of useless attributes. Here are the most common ways this happens: Treating the profile as a "one-and-done" project: The market moves too fast for static PDFs. If you haven't updated your profile since you launched, you're likely solving problems that your customers have already automated away. Focusing on interesting vs. actionable data: It's interesting that your user likes rock climbing. It's actionable that they just connected a new API integration . If a data point doesn't change how you sell, support, or build for them, keep it out of the profile. Ignoring the bad-fit profile: Sometimes, the most important part of a profile is defining who you don't want. If you don't define the "bad fit" (high support needs, low budget, the wrong tech stack), your sales team will waste time chasing leads destined to churn. Siloing the data: If Marketing has one version of the profile, Product has a second, and Customer Success has a third, your customer is experiencing three different companies stacked in a trench coat. Everyone needs to be reading from the same map, or you will confuse a buyer right out the door. Give your customer profiles new life with Zapier The value isn't just a polished document. It's in building an automated engine that fuels your lead management and CX workflows the instant a signal changes. By connecting your stack to Zapier , you can build a revenue relay: the moment a high-intent account lands on a key page, your sales rep receives a Slack alert packed with behavioral context. When a deal closes, the profile synchronizes across your CRM, support tools, and marketing systems automatically. And if a user hits a churn-risk trigger, CS gets pinged before the renewal call, not after the cancellation email. You can trigger everything automatically, or kick off workflows directly from your AI assistant. The difference between knowing something about a customer and doing something about it is the gap that Zapier closes. title: Unity Bancorp, Inc. Mourns the Passing of Director Robert ("Bobby") H. Dallas II
summary: CLINTON, N.J., Aug. 07, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) - Unity Bancorp, Inc. (NASDAQ: UNTY), parent company of Unity Bank, today announced with profound sadness the passing of Robert ("Bobby") H. Dallas II. Mr. Dallas was a founding member of the Bank and served on the Company's Board since inception and brother of Chairman David D. Dallas. He played an instrumental role in helping guide Unity from a community bank startup to one of New Jersey's strongest independent banking franchises. title: Where Your Budget Is Slipping: Fix It with Variance Analysis
summary: Track where budgets slip with variance analysis. Identify cost overruns, unfold drivers, and maintain control across UAE finance operations in real time.
body_text: Budget discussions often seem simple during planning. The complexity begins once spending flows through departments, vendors, and operational activities, where even small deviations can quickly turn into larger budget gaps. For example, the 2025 federal budget of the United Arab Emirates was approved at AED 71.5 billion, an 11.6% increase over 2024, showing how planned expenditures can shift across departments and projects. For finance leaders, variance analysis provides the visibility needed to track these changes. It helps identify where spending diverges from budgets, understand the drivers behind those deviations, and maintain financial control across departments and projects. In this blog, you’ll explore the main types of variances finance teams monitor, how budget variances are calculated, and practical techniques for analysing and managing spending deviations effectively. TL;DR Key Takeaways: Budget Deviations Often Start Across Departments: Spending flows through vendors, subscriptions, travel, and projects, making it harder to track actual costs against planned budgets. Different Variance Types Reveal Different Cost Drivers: Finance teams monitor variances in department, vendor, operational, project, and technology spend to identify where budget gaps originate. Accurate Variance Analysis Depends on Reliable Data: Complete transaction records and consistent expense categorisation ensure budget comparisons reflect real financial activity. Structured Variance Reviews Improve Financial Control: Techniques such as trend analysis, vendor analysis, and department-level reviews help finance teams identify the drivers behind spending deviations. Improves Procurement Spend Visibility: Platforms like Alaan help finance teams unify card spend, invoices, and approvals on a single platform, enabling earlier identification of procurement opportunities. 5 Types of Variances Finance Leaders Monitor Across Corporate Spend Finance leaders in the UAE track variances across corporate spend to understand where budgets deviate and identify areas of overspending or unexpected costs. Monitoring these variances in real time helps you control expenses, enforce policies, and maintain accurate, reliable financial reporting across all departments. Below are the types of variances finance leaders monitor across corporate spend. 1. Department Budget Variances Department-level variances happen when a team’s actual spending doesn’t match its allocated budget. These usually show up in areas like: Marketing campaign budgets Sales travel, and client engagement costs Operational team purchases Departmental software subscriptions For finance leaders, these variances often signal changes in business activity or gaps in budget tracking. Spotting them early lets finance teams adjust priorities and tighten budget control. 2. Vendor and Procurement Cost Variances Vendor-related variances occur when supplier costs differ from planned costs. Common causes include: Supplier price changes Extra service charges Contract updates during projects Purchases made outside negotiated agreements In sectors such as logistics, real estate , healthcare, and facilities management, procurement accounts for a large share of operational costs. Even small price changes can create noticeable gaps in budgets. Tracking these variances helps you spot inefficiencies or potential contract risks. Suggested Read: Vendor Payments in the UAE: Methods, Tools, and Best Practices 3. Operational Expense Variances Operational variances appear when day-to-day activities cost more or less than expected. Examples include: Travel and accommodation expenses Logistics and transportation costs Equipment purchases Site-level operational spending These variances often reflect shifts in operational demand or activity levels. Finance leaders need to decide whether these costs are necessary for growth or uncontrolled spending. 4. Project or Location-Based Variances Companies running multiple projects or sites often see cost deviations linked to specific units. Typical examples include: Construction or development projects Regional offices or retail locations Logistics hubs and warehouses Healthcare facilities or service centres Suggested Read: Logistics Spend Management: Best Practices and Strategies Project-level variances can come from contractor price changes, operational delays, or unexpected resource needs. Finance teams need to track these closely to keep each project financially sustainable. 5. Subscription and Technology Spend Variances Budget deviations are increasingly driven by technology spending. Common reasons include: Teams adopting new SaaS tools Upgrading existing software plans Adding user licences Growing cloud infrastructure usage Each expense may seem small on its own, but together they can push technology budgets higher than planned. For tech-driven companies, monitoring subscription-related variances is key to sound financial oversight. However, identifying these deviations consistently requires clear visibility into spending across departments, vendors, and expense categories. At Alaan , we help finance teams consolidate corporate card transactions, invoices, and expense data into one unified spend management platform. This creates a single source of truth for operational spending, making it easier to analyse budget variances without manually compiling data from multiple systems. How Finance Leaders Calculate Budget Variances in Real Financial Workflows? Finance leaders calculate budget variances by comparing actual departmental and project spend against planned budgets, using data from multiple systems and payment channels. This approach helps you identify overspending, highlight inefficiencies, and take timely corrective actions to keep operations aligned with financial goals. To apply this approach consistently, you need to use the budget variance formula to quantify differences between actual and planned spending. Budget Variance Formula At its simplest, variance analysis shows the difference between actual spending and the budgeted amount. If the result is positive, it means spending went over the budget. If the result is negative, spending stayed under the planned allocation. Finance teams calculate this at different levels, including departments, projects, and vendor-related spending. Here’s how the formula works in practice, using an operational budget scenario. A Practical Example From an Operational Budget Let’s take a UAE-based logistics company managing its monthly transportation budget. Planned transportation budget: AED 300,000 per month Actual transportation spending at month-end: AED 345,000 Applying the formula: Variance = 345,000 − 300,000 = AED 45,000 overspend This shows that transportation costs exceeded the approved budget for that month. The next step is to interpret the results during a finance review. Interpreting the Result in a Finance Review The variance number highlights how much spending deviated from the plan, but it doesn’t explain why finance leaders need to dig into operational factors behind the numbers. Common drivers include: Higher delivery demand due to increased sales Vendor price changes for logistics services Extra transportation routes or emergency shipments Operational inefficiencies affecting fuel or fleet costs By analysing these, finance teams can determine whether the overspend reflects necessary business activity or a cost control issue. But the quality of variance analysis depends on the precision of the data collected by finance teams. Why Data Accuracy Determines the Quality of Variance Analysis? The accuracy of variance analysis depends entirely on reliable financial data. Finance leaders focus on three key areas when calculating variances: Complete transaction records across departments Correct categorisation of expenses Consistent reporting across financial systems When spending is tracked consistently and reviewed regularly, variance analysis becomes a powerful tool. It helps finance teams monitor budgets, enforce discipline, and keep spending aligned with organisational priorities. Once budget variances are calculated, you can use them to guide both monthly and real-time variance analysis. 5 Steps to Conduct Variance Analysis During Monthly and Real-Time Reviews Finance leaders perform variance analysis by comparing actual spend to budget in monthly or real-time reviews to quickly identify deviations. This process helps you identify cost overruns, operational inefficiencies, and compliance gaps, enabling timely corrective action and informed financial decisions. Here's how you can conduct variance analysis during monthly and real-time reviews: 1. Consolidate Actual Spending Data The first step in any variance review is gathering accurate spending data from across the organisation. This gives a clear picture of what the company actually spent during the review period. Without complete and consistent data, variance analysis won’t be reliable. 2. Compare Actual Spending With Budget Allocations Once actual spending is consolidated, the next step is to compare it with approved budgets for the same period. These comparisons happen at different levels, such as: Department budgets Project budgets Vendor spending categories Operational cost centres This step shows where spending is on track and where deviations have occurred. 3. Identify Material Variances Finance leaders then focus on deviations that are large enough to matter, or that affect overall financial performance. Typical triggers include: Significant overspending in a department Vendor costs exceeding contract terms Operational expenses growing faster than planned Project costs going beyond the budgeted amounts Also Read: Vendor Invoice Processing: Stages, Challenges & Automation 4. Investigate the Root Cause Once a variance is spotted, finance teams dig into why it happened. They examine operational factors such as: Changes in business activity Vendor price adjustments Unexpected operational costs Spending outside approved policies This helps determine whether the variance is due to genuine business growth, operational inefficiencies, or lapses in budget control. 5. Implement Financial Adjustments Variance analysis only adds value if it leads to action. After identifying the cause, finance leaders may take steps like: Adjusting departmental spending plans Renegotiating vendor contracts Reallocating budgets between projects Strengthening approval processes for future spending These actions ensure operational spending stays aligned with financial plans. Conducting these reviews effectively often involves applying established variance analysis techniques used by modern finance teams. Top 6 Variance Analysis Techniques to Improve Budget Accuracy Modern finance teams in UAE businesses use variance analysis techniques to compare planned budgets with actual spend, highlighting discrepancies across departments and projects. These techniques help you pinpoint cost drivers, assess operational efficiency, and make data-driven decisions to maintain profitability and financial control. 1. Trend Analysis Across Financial Periods Trend analysis examines how spending changes over time rather than reviewing variances in isolation. Finance teams often track: Monthly operational spending trends Department budget usage across quarters Vendor cost changes over time Growth patterns in recurring expenses For example, if transportation costs rise gradually over several months, the variance may reflect increasing operational demand rather than a sudden overspend. Tracking trends helps you see whether a variance is a short-term fluctuation or a longer-term cost shift. 2. Department-Level Variance Analysis Another common approach is reviewing spending by department. This helps you see how each business unit is performing against its budget. Finance leaders typically examine: Marketing campaign expenditures Sales travel and client engagement costs Operational team purchases Departmental technology subscriptions Department-level analysis pinpoints where spending pressures originate and ensures each team stays accountable for its budget. 3. Vendor-Level Cost Analysis Vendor-level analysis focuses on changes in procurement spending. Since many operational costs depend on third-party suppliers, reviewing vendor transactions helps finance teams identify pricing changes or contract deviations. This often includes: Reviewing supplier invoices across financial periods Comparing contract pricing with actual charges Identifying unusual spikes in vendor spending In industries like logistics, facilities management, and real estate, vendor-level analysis is key to keeping operational costs under control. 4. Project or Cost-Centre Variance Analysis Companies running multiple projects, locations, or cost centres often analyse variances at the operational unit level. Finance teams may review: Project budgets for construction or development initiatives Operating costs for regional offices or retail locations Logistics hub expenses Facility maintenance spending This helps you see which units are driving the biggest budget deviations and evaluate each unit’s financial performance independently. 5. Volume and Activity-Based Variance Analysis Some variances happen because business activity levels change. Finance teams check whether cost deviations match operational volume. Examples include: Higher logistics costs from increased shipments Marketing expenses rising with campaign activity Customer acquisition costs growing during expansion Activity-based analysis helps finance leaders separate normal cost growth tied to business performance from true overspending. 6. Continuous Spend Monitoring Today, finance teams combine periodic variance reviews with continuous monitoring of operational spending. Instead of waiting until month-end, you track spending throughout the financial period. This lets you spot unusual transactions or emerging cost patterns early, before they significantly affect the budget. Continuous monitoring improves financial oversight, helping teams investigate variances sooner and respond faster to changes in spending. At Alaan , we enable continuous monitoring of operational spend by bringing together corporate cards, expense submissions, and approvals on a single platform. This allows finance teams to track spending against budgets throughout the financial period rather than waiting for month-end reports. Applying these techniques effectively requires applying proven strategies that improve the accuracy and efficiency of variance analysis. 6 Best Strategies Finance Leaders Use for Effective Variance Analysis Finance leaders use targeted strategies to make variance analysis more effective, ensuring budgets, departmental spend, and operational costs are closely monitored. These strategies help you detect deviations early, optimise resource allocation, and maintain control over profitability across projects and business units. 1. Prioritise High-Impact Cost Categories Variance reviews are most useful when finance teams focus on the expenses that most affect profitability. High-value areas such as procurement, logistics, technology spending, and operational overhead often drive the largest budget deviations. How to implement: Identify cost categories that make up the largest share of operational spending Focus variance reviews on vendor payments, operational costs, and major procurement items Give extra attention to expenses that directly affect profit margins Must Read: Vendor Payments in the UAE: Methods, Tools, and Best Practices 2. Compare Variances With Historical Spending Trends Looking at a variance alone can be misleading. Comparing it with past spending helps finance teams see whether the change is unusual or part of a recurring pattern. How to implement: Compare current spending with historical monthly or quarterly averages Check if similar variances occurred in previous periods Use these trends to decide if a deviation needs deeper investigation 3. Investigate Recurring Variances Some deviations continue to appear across financial periods. When the same cost category consistently goes over budget, it usually points to problems in budgeting assumptions or operational planning. How to implement: Identify expense categories that frequently exceed their budgets Check whether the original budget assumptions still match actual operational activity Adjust future budgets if recurring variances continue 4. Use Variance Insights to Improve Future Budgets Variance analysis becomes more powerful when it informs future financial planning. Lessons from past deviations help teams refine budget estimates and forecasting assumptions. How to implement: Review historical variances during annual budget preparation Adjust cost projections based on actual spending patterns from previous periods Incorporate these insights into financial forecasting models 5. Document the Cause of Major Variances Keeping a record of variance explanations helps finance teams see patterns over time. These records become a valuable reference for future reviews and investigations. How to implement: Document the operational reason behind significant budget deviations Maintain records of variance explanations for recurring expense categories Refer to these historical explanations during future financial reviews. These strategies are most impactful when paired with a platform that simplifies and strengthens variance analysis. How Alaan Helps Finance Teams Strengthen Variance Analysis? Many UAE finance teams perform monthly variance analysis, but fragmented spending across cards, invoices, subscriptions, and departments often limits real-time visibility and delays detection of budget deviations. At Alaan , we bring corporate cards, expense capture, approvals, and accounting integrations on a single platform. This continuous visibility helps you monitor spending against budgets, quickly investigate variances, and maintain stronger financial control. What Alaan Covers Across the Operational Spend Lifecycle Accurate, timely visibility into operational spending drives effective variance analysis. At Alaan, we empower finance teams to analyse budget deviations with reliable financial data by strengthening every stage of the spend lifecycle. 1. Corporate Cards With Built-In Spend Controls At Alaan, we offer corporate cards with configurable spend controls so finance teams can manage spending before it affects budgets. Admins can: Set spending limits by employee, team, or project Restrict merchant categories based on company policies Issue virtual or physical cards instantly Freeze or block cards in real time These controls help ensure operational expenses stay within approved budgets and reduce the risk of unplanned spending that could create budget variances. 2. Automated Expense Capture and Receipt Verification Once a payment is made using a corporate card, the transaction appears instantly in the platform, and the employee uploads the receipt. Alaan Intelligence automatically extracts key data such as: Vendor name Transaction amount Invoice details Date and time of purchase The system then verifies this information against the transaction record and flags any discrepancies. This ensures finance teams work with accurate expense data during variance analysis. 3. Structured Approval Workflows Before Expenses Are Finalised Expenses and invoices move through policy-driven approval workflows aligned with company spending rules. This ensures: Expenses are reviewed before being finalised Spending aligns with departmental budgets Unusual or policy exceptions are flagged early By enforcing approvals upstream, finance teams prevent unapproved spending that often leads to unexpected budget variances. 4. Accounting Integration for Accurate Financial Records At Alaan, we integrate directly with accounting systems such as: NetSuite QuickBooks Xero Microsoft Dynamics Once an expense is approved, the transaction automatically syncs with the accounting system. This reduces manual data entry and ensures finance teams analyse variances using accurate financial records. 5. Real-Time Visibility Into Operational Spending We provide live dashboards that show: Corporate card transactions Department-level spending Submitted and pending expenses Operational spending trends This visibility helps finance teams track how actual spending compares with budgets throughout the financial period rather than discovering deviations only during month-end reviews. What Alaan Is (And Is Not) Alaan is a spend management platform designed to strengthen financial control over operational expenses. It helps finance teams: Control spending through corporate cards and policy enforcement Capture and verify expenses automatically Maintain accurate, real-time financial records Alaan does not replace your accounting or ERP system . Instead, it integrates with your existing tools to improve upstream spend control and provide the visibility finance teams need to monitor budget variances effectively. Final Thoughts Variance analysis provides finance leaders with a clear view of how spending aligns with budgets. For UAE businesses, it helps spot deviations early, understand their causes, and keep departmental spending on track. Accurate, real-time visibility across departments, vendors, and projects boosts financial discipline and improves budgeting. Take action now to transform your finance operations! FAQs 1. What are the benefits of variance analysis for finance teams? Variance analysis helps finance leaders spot where actual spending differs from the budget. It allows teams to quickly identify overspending, operational inefficiencies, or unexpected cost drivers. In growing organisations, 2. What is the difference between favourable and unfavourable variance? A favourable variance happens when spending is lower than planned or revenue exceeds expectations. An unfavourable variance occurs when costs go over budget or revenue falls short, signalling the need for a closer financial review. 3. What is the column method for variance analysis? The column method puts budgeted values, actual values, and the calculated variance side by side in reports. This makes it easy for finance teams to compare planned versus actual performance across departments, projects, or cost categories. 4. What role do standards play in variance analysis? Standards are benchmark costs or performance targets used during budgeting and planning. Finance teams compare actual spending against these standards to identify deviations and check whether spending aligns with expected performance. 5. How often should finance teams perform variance analysis? Most finance teams review variances during the monthly financial close to compare actual spending with the budget. title: Rapid Micro Biosystems Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
summary: Reports second quarter 2026 total revenue of $8.1 million, representing 11% growth compared to the second quarter of 2025 Achieved a significant milestone with the 200th Growth Direct system placed globally; placed four Growth Direct systems and completed nine validations in the second quarter
body_text: Reports second quarter 2026 total revenue of $8.1 million , representing 11% growth compared to the second quarter of 2025 Achieved a significant milestone with the 200th Growth Direct system placed globally; placed four Growth Direct systems and completed nine validations in the second quarter 2026 Second quarter consumable revenue increased more than 20% year-over-year Second quarter recurring revenue increased 14% year-over-year; comprised 63% of total revenue Reports record second quarter total gross margin of 15% , an increase of 11 percentage points compared to the second quarter of 2025 Merck MilliporeSigma to host European Growth Direct Day in October 2026, supporting customer engagement, education, and commercial pipeline development across Europe Reaffirms full year 2026 total revenue guidance range of $37.0 million to $41.0 million, including 30 to 38 Growth Direct system placements Reaffirms full year 2026 gross margin percentage guidance of approximately 20%, with second half 2026 margins in the mid-20% range LEXINGTON, Mass., Aug. 07, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rapid Micro Biosystems, Inc. (Nasdaq: RPID) (the “Company”), an innovative life sciences technology company providing mission critical automation solutions to facilitate the efficient manufacturing and fast, safe release of healthcare products, today announced its financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. "Our second quarter results reflect continued execution against the strategic and financial priorities we outlined at the beginning of the year," said Robert Spignesi, President and CEO. "Total revenue increased 11%, recurring revenue grew 14% and consumables achieved quarterly records in both units and revenue. Importantly, we delivered record second-quarter total gross margin of 15%, marking a positive inflection that reflects meaningful progress against our margin expansion initiatives and supports our path to positive cash flow." Spignesi continued, "As we look to the second half of 2026, we remain encouraged by strong customer engagement, continued momentum in multi-system and enterprise deployment opportunities, and an expanding contribution from our collaboration with MilliporeSigma. Combined with favorable industry tailwinds, including increased adoption of automation and ongoing U.S. reshoring and biomanufacturing capacity expansion, we believe we are well positioned to achieve our full-year objectives and enter 2027 with positive momentum." Second Quarter Financial Results Total revenue for the second quarter of 2026 increased 10.9% to $8.1 million compared to $7.3 million in the second quarter of 2025. The Company placed four new Growth Direct® systems and completed the validation of nine customer systems compared to four placements and two validations in the second quarter of 2025. Product revenue increased 10.1% to $5.3 million, compared to $4.8 million in the second quarter of 2025. Service revenue increased 12.5% to $2.8 million, compared to $2.5 million in the second quarter of 2025. Recurring revenue increased 14.3% to $5.0 million, compared to $4.4 million in the second quarter of 2025. Total cost of revenue was $6.8 million in the second quarter of 2026, a decrease of 2.1% compared to $7.0 million in the second quarter of 2025. Gross margin was 15.0%, or $1.2 million, a quarterly record, compared to 3.8%, or $0.3 million in the second quarter of 2025. Total operating expenses increased by 8.9% to $13.5 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $12.4 million in the second quarter of 2025. General and administrative expenses increased by 11.3%, research and development expenses increased by 3.2%, and sales and marketing expenses increased by 10.3%, in each case compared to the second quarter of 2025. Net loss for the second quarter of 2026 was $12.9 million and net loss per share was $0.27, compared to a net loss of $11.9 million and net loss per share of $0.27 in the second quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA loss for the second quarter of 2026 was $10.3 million, compared to a loss of $10.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. Cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments were approximately $20 million as of June 30, 2026. Full Year 2026 Outlook The Company is reaffirming its full year 2026 total revenue guidance range of $37.0 million to $41.0 million including a range of 30 to 38 Growth Direct system placements and total gross margin percentage of approximately 20%. The Company is increasing its full year 2026 system validation guidance to at least 27 validations, up from 25 previously. Webcast Details The Company will host a conference call before the market opens today, August 7, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. ET to discuss its second quarter 2026 financial results. The live call is accessible on the Company’s website at investors.rapidmicrobio.com and will be archived and available for replay for one year. About Rapid Micro Biosystems Rapid Micro Biosystems is an innovative life sciences technology company providing mission critical automation solutions to facilitate the efficient manufacturing and fast, safe release of healthcare products such as biologics, vaccines, cell and gene therapies, and sterile injectables. The Company’s flagship Growth Direct system automates and modernizes the antiquated, manual microbial quality control (“MQC”) testing workflows used in the largest and most complex pharmaceutical manufacturing operations across the globe. The Growth Direct system brings the quality control lab to the manufacturing floor, unlocking the power of MQC automation to deliver the faster results, greater accuracy, increased operational efficiency, better compliance with data integrity regulations, and quicker decision making that customers rely on to ensure safe and consistent supply of important healthcare products. The Company is headquartered in Lexington, Massachusetts and has U.S. manufacturing in Lowell, Massachusetts, with global locations in Switzerland, Germany, and the Netherlands. For more information, please visit www.rapidmicrobio.com or follow the Company on X (formerly known as Twitter) at @rapidmicrobio or on LinkedIn. title: Bancarización alta, penetración baja: la pregunta central para Chile
summary: Chile tiene la bancarización más alta de LATAM , pero solo un tercio usa crédito, ahorro o gestión de su dinero. Así lo vivimos en Truora Nights Chile
body_text: “Tener la cuenta abierta no significa tener un cliente activo.” Esa fue la tensión con la que se armó el panel “Confianza Digital: el reto del sector financiero chileno” , durante el primer Truora Nights Chile, con tres modelos que se sentaron a resolver la misma pregunta desde ángulos distintos: BICE , banco tradicional en plena digitalización; ProntoPaga , la fintech de pagos que ahora escala a neobanco regional con YOL1; y Tapp , la tarjeta digital de Caja Los Andes. El dato de partida: Chile tiene el 87,1% de su población bancarizada , la tasa más alta de América Latina. Pero solo un tercio de ese grupo accede realmente a crédito, ahorro o gestión activa de su dinero . El acceso ya está resuelto. La profundidad, no El problema ya no es el acceso, es la penetración Durante años, la conversación sobre inclusión financiera en Chile giró en torno a una sola pregunta: ¿cuánta gente tiene una cuenta? Esa pregunta ya se respondió. El 97% de la población tiene acceso a algún producto financiero formal , según datos de País Digital. El reto se movió a otro lugar: la mayoría de los bancarizados no va mucho más allá de tener una cuenta abierta. Los números lo confirman con crudeza. Según el Banco Mundial, de los chilenos bancarizados, solo un 24% pidió un crédito formal en el último año, a pesar de que abrir una cuenta hoy toma entre 5 y 10 minutos. La cuenta está. El salto al segundo producto, no. Esa es exactamente la pregunta que estructuró la noche: cómo lograr que cada cliente use más productos financieros, no cómo conseguir más clientes. Un ecosistema que crece rápido, en un país que no Chile cerró 2026 con 557 empresas fintech operando, un 15,3% más que las 483 de 2024 , según el Mapa Fintech Chile 2026 de FinteChile, EY y Finnovista. La tasa de mortalidad fue de apenas 6,3%, señal de que la industria ya pasó de la etapa de validación a la de consolidación. Y sin embargo, en el Chile Fintech Forum 2026 el diagnóstico fue casi paradójico : el país tiene la infraestructura para liderar la economía digital de la región, pero crece a un ritmo de apenas 1,5% a 2,5% anual. Toda la tecnología está. El motor no siempre arranca. Ese contraste, entre un ecosistema técnicamente maduro y una adopción de producto que no despega al mismo ritmo, es el que banca, fintech y cajas enfrentan desde tres posiciones distintas. La misma pregunta, tres terrenos distintos A cada speaker se le planteó ese mismo problema, pero desde su propio terreno. Esto es lo que se sabe de cada uno, más allá de lo que se haya dicho esa noche sobre el escenario: A BICE se le preguntó algo directo: por qué, si los usuarios ya prefieren los canales digitales, siguen existiendo procesos que dependen de la presencialidad o de la asesoría de una persona en sucursal. Es una pregunta que conecta con una decisión que el banco ya tomó, independiente del panel: integrar la infraestructura de identidad digital. Bajo el liderazgo de innovación de BICE, BICECORP abrió una vertical regtech con Amparo ID , una solución de autenticación digital que venden a terceros como producto de marca blanca, embebible como SDK o en formato standalone, con clientes ya en Uruguay. Un banco que decidió no solo resolver su propio onboarding, sino convertir esa capacidad en un producto que vende. A ProntoPaga se le preguntó por el salto que están dando ahora mismo: de resolver un problema puntual, procesar pagos, a convertirse en infraestructura financiera completa. Ese salto ya tiene nombre propio, con o sin panel de por medio: YOL1, el neobanco regional que la compañía lanzó para pasar del B2B al B2C , moviendo dinero entre países con medios locales como PIX en Brasil, YAPE en Perú o QR interoperables en Argentina. En mayo de 2026, YOL1 compró el negocio de tarjetas de Inversiones La Polar , una jugada que le ahorra al grupo cerca de dos años de trámites de licencias ante la CMF. A Tapp se le preguntó por el reto más difícil de su base: cómo acercar productos financieros por canal digital sin dejar atrás al afiliado no digital, como el adulto mayor. Es una pregunta que conecta directo con el diseño del producto: Tapp es una tarjeta prepago digital con foco explícito en salud financiera , pensada para que el usuario controle sus fondos en vez de que las cuotas o los intereses lo controlen a él, apuntando tanto a segmentos no bancarizados como a jóvenes en su primera experiencia laboral. Tres empresas, tres estrategias de producto distintas frente a la misma pregunta: cómo profundizar la relación con un cliente que ya tiene acceso, sin perder lo que cada una construyó para ganarse su lugar. La confianza también es una norma y un estandar en chile Hay un ángulo que conecta directo con todo esto, y que cayó justo dos días después del panel. Desde el 1 de agosto de 2026, la Norma de Carácter General 538 de la CMF exige que bancos, emisores de tarjetas, cooperativas y fintechs reguladas apliquen autenticación reforzada , con al menos dos factores independientes, en procesos críticos como transferencias, onboarding digital y cambios de datos sensibles. El punto clave: la responsabilidad no se terceriza. La institución responde por el cumplimiento aunque use tecnología de un proveedor externo. Es la misma lógica regulatoria detrás de la Ley 21.719 de protección de datos personales , que ya cubrimos en nuestro blog: la identidad y los datos de un cliente son responsabilidad de la institución, no algo que se terceriza sin más. La urgencia detrás de esa norma tiene números que la respaldan. Según la Abif, los reclamos por fraude en la banca chilena se duplicaron en 2024 , y la tasa sigue siendo tres veces más alta que antes de la Ley de Fraudes de 2020, más de seis veces el promedio europeo. Solo en el primer semestre de 2025, la banca recibió reclamos asociados a 170 mil clientes. Profundizar la relación con el cliente, la pregunta que armó la noche, no se puede resolver a costa de bajar la guardia frente al fraude. Es la misma tensión que ya resolvió BICE al construir Amparo ID: la identidad digital no es solo un trámite de cumplimiento, es la base sobre la que se puede construir cualquier producto nuevo Si quieres revisar cómo se ve hoy la validación de identidad frente a la normativa vigente en Chile, puedes hacer nuestro diagnóstico de la Ley 21.719 . Cierre: el acceso ya se ganó, ahora hay que ganarse el uso Banca, fintech y cajas se sentaron en Truora Nights Chile a resolver la misma pregunta desde tres puntos de partida distintos: la etapa de convencer a alguien de abrir una cuenta ya terminó. La que sigue, convencerlo de usar más de un producto sin perder la confianza que costó ganarse, recién empieza, y va a definir qué actor del ecosistema financiero chileno crece los próximos cinco años y cuál se queda solo con la cuenta abierta. Si quieres revisar cómo se ve hoy la validación de identidad frente a la normativa vigente en Chile, puedes hacer nuestro diagnóstico de la Ley 21.719 .

title: New Authority Checklist 3: Cover Your Assets (Insurance)
body_text: Step 3: Get insurance coverage Now that you have your company and equipment set up, you’re just a couple steps away from getting your business running. But before you hit the open road, you’ll need to make sure you have the right insurance policy that fits your needs. Minimum insurance requirements The FMCSA (Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration) requires specific insurance coverage. Auto Liability Insurance is a primary requirement, with coverage amounts varying based on the type of goods transported: Non-Hazardous Cargo: $750,000 Hazardous Cargo: $1,000,000 Portable Tanks: $5,000,000 You will need to submit various forms to the FMCSA through your insurance company to obtain an MC number, such as: BMC-91 - public liability insurance BOC-3 - processing agents MCS-90 - endorsement that creates an obligation to pay any judgment resulting from negligence of operations Auto Liability Insurance covers damages to property and body caused by your truck. Cargo Insurance covers damages to the goods you haul. When you take possession of cargo, you are liable for any damages that happen until you deliver. Physical Damage Coverage covers the cost of repair to your vehicle in case of accident, theft, fire, weather, or vandalism. This coverage is usually required if you finance your truck, and strongly recommended even if you own your truck outright. Auto liability insurance and cargo insurance are mandatory to work with brokers and shippers. Additional lines of insurance Here is a list of other types of insurance, in order of what is most commonly held by small carriers. General Liability Insurance protects you in claims for bodily injury, personal injury, property damage liability, advertising injury liability, medical payments, product & completed operations, and seven days or less coverage for damage to rented properties. Non-Trucking Liability Insurance provides coverage for the use of a tractor for non-business purposes. Bobtail Insurance provides protection for a tractor when it is operated without a trailer, whether under load or not. This can often be confused with Non-Trucking Liability Insurance, which covers your vehicle when you are using it for personal use. Trailer Interchange Agreement Insurance provides coverage for damage to non-owned trailers when they receive physical damage while under a trailer interchange agreement. This is usually required for drop-and-hook work. Passenger Accident Insurance provides coverage for the driver if a truck accident occurs while an uninsured passenger is in the vehicle. Mechanical Breakdown Insurance offers coverage for out-of-pocket expenses related to repairs of the insured vehicle. Optional Downtime Coverage takes effect when your commercial truck undergoes downtime, such as during repairs or maintenance. Limited Depreciation Coverage helps cover the gap between the fair market value that the insurance will likely pay out and what you owe on the vehicle or the cost to replace the vehicle. On-Hook Coverage provides coverage for vehicles that are not owned by your business during towing or hauling. When entering the trucking industry, it is a requirement to purchase insurance to work with brokers and to protect you from unexpected factors. While the minimums have been set by FMCSA and brokerage companies, you will likely want to purchase more coverage depending on your operations. Having only the minimums in place may not be enough to fully protect you, so discuss this with your insurance company. Investing in an appropriate policy can save you money in the long run and provide peace of mind while on the road. ‍ Continue the New Authority Checklist series below: New Authority Checklist 1: First Things First (Business Setup) New Authority Checklist 2: Choose Your Player (Equipment) New Authority Checklist 4: Show Me The Money (Invoicing & Factoring) ‍ About TrueNorth TrueNorth pioneers a new era for truckers, new carriers, and owner-operators. Born from a legacy of trucking roots, it transforms the industry's landscape with a cutting-edge operating system. By replacing outdated processes with a unified mobile app, TrueNorth empowers truckers with superpowers – a dispatcher, CRM, financial dashboard, and real-time market insights. Bridging the gap between traditional fleets and tech companies, TrueNorth champions truckers' profitability, offering tools, and support for streamlined operations. In a world where autonomy looms, TrueNorth remains the ally ensuring profits and efficiency for the heroes steering the wheels of commerce. Get started with TrueNorth today , and see how a trucker-first tech platform can revolutionize your operations.
